text: Which dinosaur had three horns and a large bony frill?
explanation: Triceratops had two long horns above its eyes, a shorter nose horn, and a bony frill behind its head.
hint: Look for a dinosaur with a special head shape.
source: Natural History Museum, London — Dino Directory

text: What kind of food did Tyrannosaurus rex eat?
explanation: Tyrannosaurus rex was a carnivore: a meat-eating dinosaur. Its powerful jaws and sharp teeth were suited to eating other animals.
hint: Think about what sharp teeth can help an animal eat.
source: Natural History Museum, London — Dino Directory

text: Which dinosaur had large plates along its back?
explanation: Stegosaurus had two rows of bony plates along its back and spikes on its tail. Scientists still study what the plates were used for.
hint: Think about the shapes along the dinosaur’s back.
source: Natural History Museum, London — Dino Directory

text: Which of these dinosaurs had a very long neck?
explanation: Brachiosaurus was a long-necked, plant-eating dinosaur. Its front legs were longer than its back legs, giving its body a sloping shape.
hint: Compare the body shapes of these dinosaurs.
source: Natural History Museum, London — Dino Directory

text: Which dinosaur had a heavy bony club at the end of its tail?
explanation: Ankylosaurus had armour on its body and a bony tail club. The club could be used for defence.
hint: Look for a dinosaur with body armour.
source: Natural History Museum, London — Dino Directory

text: What did Diplodocus eat?
explanation: Diplodocus was a herbivore, which means a plant eater. It had a long neck, a long tail, and peg-like teeth.
hint: Its teeth helped it gather food, rather than tear meat.
source: Natural History Museum, London — Dino Directory

text: Which dinosaur had tall back spines that formed a sail-like shape?
explanation: Spinosaurus had tall spines on its back that formed a sail-like shape. Scientists are still investigating how it used this feature.
hint: Think about a dinosaur with an unusual outline.
source: Natural History Museum, London — Dino Directory

text: Which dinosaur had a pointed spike on each thumb?
explanation: Iguanodon had a large spike on each thumb. It was a plant-eating dinosaur with hands that were very different from ours.
hint: Think about a feature on a dinosaur’s hand.
source: Natural History Museum, London — Dino Directory

text: How many legs did Tyrannosaurus rex walk on?
explanation: Tyrannosaurus rex walked on its two powerful back legs. Its arms were much smaller than its legs.
hint: Compare its arms with its back legs.
source: Natural History Museum, London — Dino Directory

text: Which food would suit a plant-eating Triceratops?
explanation: Triceratops was a herbivore. Its beak and teeth helped it eat plants, even though it had impressive horns.
hint: Horns do not tell us what an animal eats.
source: Natural History Museum, London — Dino Directory

text: What does the word herbivore mean?

choices.text: An animal that eats only rocks

explanation: A herbivore eats plants. Dinosaurs such as Diplodocus and Triceratops were herbivores.
hint: Think about how scientists group animals by their food.

text: Which feature helped Tyrannosaurus rex tear meat?
explanation: Tyrannosaurus rex had large, sharp teeth and powerful jaws suited to feeding on other animals.
hint: Think about the shape that helps cut tough food.

text: Where were the long defensive spikes of Stegosaurus?
explanation: Stegosaurus had long spikes on its tail. These could help it defend itself against an attacker.
hint: Its back plates and its spikes were different structures.

text: Which dinosaur was protected by bony body armour?
explanation: Ankylosaurus had bony armour covering much of its body, as well as a tail club.
hint: Compare the outer covering of these animals.

text: Which dinosaur had front legs longer than its back legs?
explanation: Brachiosaurus had unusually long front legs. Its body sloped up towards its shoulders and long neck.
hint: Picture how each animal stood.

text: Fish were part of the diet of which dinosaur?
explanation: Spinosaurus had a long snout and cone-shaped teeth. Fossil evidence supports fish as part of its diet.
hint: Think about teeth that could help grip slippery food.

text: How did dinosaurs produce their young?
explanation: Dinosaurs laid eggs. Fossil eggs and nests provide evidence of this, and their living relatives, birds, also lay eggs.
hint: Think about how birds and other reptiles reproduce.

text: How were the back legs of dinosaurs generally positioned?

choices.text: Spread sideways like a sprawling lizard

explanation: Dinosaurs generally stood with their back legs under their bodies. This upright stance distinguishes them from sprawling reptiles.
hint: Think about how an animal supports its weight.

text: Which group were flying reptiles rather than dinosaurs?
explanation: Pterosaurs were flying reptiles related to dinosaurs, but they were a separate group. Birds, in contrast, are dinosaurs.
hint: Not every prehistoric reptile belongs to the same group.

text: What did Triceratops use its beak and teeth to eat?
explanation: Triceratops used its beak and teeth to eat plants. Its horns do not mean that it was a meat eater.
hint: An impressive head can have more than one job.

text: In which period did dinosaurs first appear?
explanation: The earliest dinosaurs appeared during the Triassic Period, before the Jurassic and Cretaceous.
hint: Think about which of the dinosaur-age periods came first.

text: Which order puts these periods from oldest to youngest?
explanation: The Mesozoic Era is divided into the Triassic, then the Jurassic, then the Cretaceous.
hint: Start with the earliest dinosaur-age period.

text: Which period did Stegosaurus live in?
explanation: Stegosaurus lived in the Late Jurassic. It lived many millions of years before Tyrannosaurus rex.
hint: The dinosaur age lasted a very long time.

text: Which period did Tyrannosaurus rex live in?
explanation: Tyrannosaurus rex lived near the end of the Cretaceous Period, long after dinosaurs first appeared.
hint: Place it towards the end of the non-bird dinosaur age.

text: Why could a living Stegosaurus not have met a living Tyrannosaurus rex?

choices.text: Stegosaurus lived only in the ocean
They lived millions of years apart
Tyrannosaurus rex lived before all dinosaurs

explanation: Stegosaurus lived in the Late Jurassic, while Tyrannosaurus rex lived in the Late Cretaceous. Their lifetimes did not overlap.
hint: Compare when each dinosaur lived.

text: Tyrannosaurus rex fossils are known from which continent?
explanation: Tyrannosaurus rex lived in what is now North America. Fossils from this region tell us about its Late Cretaceous world.
hint: Think about where its known fossils have been found.

text: Velociraptor fossils have been found in which of these countries?
explanation: Velociraptor fossils are known from Mongolia, in Asia. It was much smaller than the raptors often shown in films.
hint: Think about the deserts of central Asia.

text: In which country were Argentinosaurus fossils discovered?
explanation: Argentinosaurus fossils were found in Argentina, South America. It was a very large sauropod, but its exact size is uncertain.
hint: Consider where the fossils were discovered, rather than guessing the animal’s size.

text: What was the large supercontinent of the Triassic called?
explanation: During the Triassic, the continents were joined in a huge landmass called Pangaea. It later broke into smaller landmasses.
hint: Imagine many continents connected together.

text: About when did the end-Cretaceous extinction occur?
explanation: The end-Cretaceous extinction occurred about 66 million years ago. Non-bird dinosaurs disappeared, but birds survived.
hint: The event was long before modern humans appeared.

text: What does a palaeontologist study?
explanation: Palaeontologists study ancient life, including dinosaurs, using fossils and their geological context.
hint: Think about the evidence left by organisms from the past.

text: Which is a trace fossil showing an animal’s activity?
explanation: A footprint is a trace fossil: evidence of an activity. Teeth, skulls and shells are body fossils.
hint: Look for evidence of something an animal did.

text: In which type of rock are fossils usually found?
explanation: Fossils are usually found in sedimentary rocks, formed from layers of mud, sand, silt or other sediment.
hint: Think about rock made from layers of settled material.

text: What often happens to buried bones during fossilisation?

choices.text: Minerals replace or fill parts of them

explanation: During fossilisation, minerals can replace original material or fill spaces in buried remains. Not every fossil forms in the same way.
hint: Consider what groundwater can carry into buried material.

text: Which of these is a living dinosaur?
explanation: Birds are living dinosaurs. They evolved within the theropod dinosaur group; crocodiles are relatives outside the dinosaur group.
hint: Consider the evolutionary family tree of each animal.

text: Which fossil discovery supports the link between birds and other dinosaurs?
explanation: Feathered theropod fossils support the evolutionary connection between birds and other dinosaurs, alongside many shared skeletal features.
hint: Look for a body covering also found in living birds.

text: Which dinosaur group includes both Tyrannosaurus rex and modern birds?
explanation: Tyrannosaurus rex and birds belong to the theropod group. Birds evolved within one branch of theropods, not directly from Tyrannosaurus rex.
hint: Compare their evolutionary groups, not just their sizes.

text: Why record the rock layer and location of a fossil?

choices.text: To decide its colour from the map
To prove all fossils have the same age
To understand its age and surroundings

explanation: A fossil’s rock layer and location give scientists evidence about its age and ancient environment. Removing it without a record loses important context.
hint: The rock around a fossil is evidence too.

text: Which parts are generally most likely to be preserved as fossils?

choices.text: Hard parts such as teeth and bones

explanation: Hard parts such as bones, teeth and shells are more likely to survive fossilisation than soft tissues. This makes the fossil record incomplete.
hint: Think about which materials are more durable after death.

text: What is a coprolite?
explanation: A coprolite is fossilised poo. It can contain clues about ancient animals and their diets.
hint: Some fossils preserve evidence of everyday activities.

text: A scientist finds one fossil footprint, with no bones nearby. Which conclusion is safest?

choices.text: The exact species is always known
An animal left a track, but its exact species may be uncertain
Its whole life story is known

explanation: A footprint records an animal’s activity. Without more evidence, scientists may not be able to identify the exact species that made it.
hint: Separate what the evidence shows from what it cannot show.

text: Why can’t scientists usually work out skin colour from dinosaur bones alone?

choices.text: All dinosaurs were the same colour
Bones usually lack the original skin pigment evidence

explanation: Bones alone usually do not preserve skin colour. In rare fossils, special evidence such as preserved pigment structures can help researchers investigate colour.
hint: Think about where an animal’s colour comes from.

text: A dinosaur fossil has feathers. What can we conclude from that fact alone?

choices.text: It had feathers, but it did not necessarily fly
It was definitely a modern bird
It could not have lived on land

explanation: Feathers existed in dinosaurs before the evolution of modern birds. Finding feathers alone does not prove that an animal could fly.
hint: A feature can have more than one use.

text: Why is Dimetrodon excluded from the dinosaur group?

choices.text: It belonged to the separate synapsid lineage
It was another name for Spinosaurus

explanation: Dimetrodon belonged to the synapsid lineage, the broader evolutionary group that also includes mammals. It lived before dinosaurs and was not one.
hint: Similar-looking back features do not prove close relationships.

text: Which of these was an extinct marine reptile rather than a dinosaur?
explanation: Ichthyosaurus was an ichthyosaur, a group of marine reptiles outside the dinosaur group. Living swimming birds are dinosaurs, so habitat alone is not enough to classify an animal.
hint: Use evolutionary groups rather than just where an animal lived.

text: The same short-lived index fossil occurs in two rock layers far apart. What does this suggest?

choices.text: The rocks must have the same colour
The rocks contain the same dinosaur species
The layers formed at roughly the same time

explanation: Index fossils come from organisms that were widespread but existed for a relatively short geological time. They help scientists compare the ages of rock layers.
hint: Think about why a widespread fossil with a narrow time range is useful.

text: Why does the fossil record give an incomplete picture of ancient life?

choices.text: Many organisms decayed without becoming fossils
All fossils formed in one day

explanation: Fossilisation requires suitable conditions. Many organisms decayed, and soft parts were especially unlikely to survive, so much evidence is missing.
hint: Compare dying with being preserved: they are not the same event.

text: Which statement best describes the relationship between birds and dinosaurs?
explanation: Birds evolved within a branch of theropod dinosaurs. They are living dinosaurs, and pterosaurs were a separate reptile group.
hint: Think about the branch that contains feathered dinosaurs.

text: A Spinosaurus fossil has tall back spines. Which claim is directly supported?

choices.text: The sail was always bright red
It had tall back spines; their exact function needs more evidence
The sail acted exactly like a boat sail
Every dinosaur had the same spines

explanation: Tall back spines are an observed anatomical feature of Spinosaurus. Proposed functions of its sail-like structure need additional evidence and remain subjects of research.
hint: Distinguish a preserved structure from an explanation of its use.

text: What should scientists do when reliable new fossils challenge an old explanation?

choices.text: Recheck and update the explanation using the evidence

explanation: Scientific explanations are tested against evidence. New fossils can lead researchers to revise ideas about dinosaur appearance, behaviour and relationships.
hint: Good explanations must fit the available evidence.
